# HISTOR snapshot 2026-10-26: what MCP servers advertise, and when it changes

HISTOR reads the tool list (`tools/list`) of every remote MCP server in the official MCP registry on a polling schedule, and of npm/PyPI MCP packages run in a sandbox once per published version (new versions first, a few hundred a day). It records the exact tool definitions, pins them by digest, and writes a signed label to a public RFC 9162 Merkle log whenever a tool set first appears, stays the same, or changes. This snapshot is that record as files.

  * 85,913 listed servers (34,171 remote endpoints, 51,742 packages), plus 3,364 delisted
  * 40,738 with a recorded tool set; 11,528 changed at least once
  * 31,660 recorded changes, 2026-09-24 to 2026-10-26
  * 66,649 distinct tool sets (current ones and every one a change replaced)
  * 752 servers with a block-tier WARDEN pattern match, 15,273 advise-only

Live view and per-server pages: https://histor.modelmarket.dev · code: https://github.com/alexar76/histor

## What it is not

  * A tool list is what a server advertised to an anonymous client on that day. Servers that need credentials, or that refused HISTOR, have no tool set here (`lastStatus`, `skipReason` say why).
  * Pattern matches and classifier flags point at text worth reading; they do not say a server is malicious.
  * A change is a change in the definitions, not a judgement of it. Most are ordinary releases.

## Cite

Artamokhov, A. (2026). HISTOR snapshot 2026-10-26: MCP tool definitions and how they change [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23512759

This is the DOI of every snapshot (it resolves to the newest; each has its own version DOI on the record): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23512759. Also on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/alexar76/histor-mcp-tool-definitions (tag `snapshot-2026-10-26`).

## License and rights

The compilation, digests, labels, scans and verdicts are CC-BY-4.0. Tool names, descriptions and schemas are reproduced as each server published them; their rights stay with their authors. They are included so the definitions can be studied and checked. A server operator who wants out: open an issue on https://github.com/alexar76/histor with the endpoint or host. Opted-out servers are left out of every later snapshot.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## About

Monthly snapshots of a public transparency log covering remote MCP servers in the official registry and npm and PyPI MCP packages. The files hold the tool definitions each server served, every recorded change field by field, pattern scan matches, and advisory classifier readings. A signed manifest lists checksums so users can verify files, and the data is released under CC BY 4.0.

## What it does

The site says HISTOR reads the tool list of every remote server in the official MCP registry each day and runs each new npm and PyPI MCP package version in a sandbox. It presents its pattern matches and classifier flags as leads worth reading, not as proof that a server is malicious.

### Stated on the product site

License
    CC BY 4.0

Release cadence
    A full snapshot published as files once a month

Verification
    A manifest of file checksums, signed with Ed25519

Mirrors
    Hugging Face with one tag per snapshot, Zenodo with a DOI per snapshot

Coverage limit
    Servers that require a key show less or nothing to the anonymous client

Code link
    The page links a GitHub repository for the project

### Not stated on the site

  * The page does not name the LLM behind the advisory classifier readings.
  * The page does not say what the sandbox run of a package records beyond its tool list.
  * How server operators' opt-out requests are handled beyond opening an issue is not described on the page.

Written from the product site at histor.modelmarket.dev.

# 45% of remote MCP servers changed their tool definitions in four weeks. The log is now a dataset.

#mcp #security #opensource #dataset

A client that connects an MCP server reads its tool definitions: names, descriptions and input schemas. The model then reads them as instructions. Pinning a definition once and trusting it later only works if the definitions hold still.

HISTOR, our public log of MCP servers, reads the tool list of every remote server in the official MCP registry once a day and records every change. As of today the whole record is downloadable as files. Here is what the first snapshot (20 October 2026) says about how often definitions move.

## Half of them move

Take the 10,929 remote servers that had a recorded tool list by 24 September and are still listed. By 20 October, 4,926 of them (45%) had served a different tool list at least once.

  * 2,036 changed the description of a tool they already had.
  * 1,180 added a tool; 336 removed one.

# What an MCP server's tool list costs: we counted the tokens of 34,374 of them

#opensource #ai #llm #mcp

Under our survey of 12,915 MCP servers, a reader did the arithmetic we had not: 182,157 tool definitions over 7,656 servers is about 24 tools each, and a client resends every one of them with each model request. Count the tokens of a typical list, the comment said, and that becomes a cost.

HISTOR, our public log of MCP servers, keeps the current tool list of every server it observes. So instead of one typical list we counted all of them: 18,204 npm and PyPI packages and 16,170 remote servers, as of 19 October 2026.

## How we counted

A list is counted the way a client puts it into a model request: for each tool its `name`, `description` and `input_schema`, as compact JSON. The tokenizer is `o200k_base` (tiktoken 0.12). Every server with at least one tool counts once, with the list HISTOR last observed.

# We found 331 MCP tool-list changes in one week that only moved a date. Each one costs a prompt-cache write

Posted on Nov 3 • Originally published at modelmarket.dev

A reader of our last post, Paul Irolla, who builds a token optimizer for coding agents, pointed out something we had only looked at as a correctness problem. A model request starts with the tool list. Change one byte of a tool definition and every prompt cache built on that request is gone, even if the change means nothing.

HISTOR, our public log of MCP tool definitions, records every change it sees, so we counted. In the week of 25 October to 1 November it recorded 10,712 changes to the tool lists of 4,491 MCP servers. 331 of them changed nothing but a date or a timestamp.

With Anthropic's API, the cached prefix is built in a fixed order: tools first, then the system prompt, then the messages. A change anywhere in the tools invalidates everything after it. Reading a cached prefix costs a tenth of the normal input price. Writing one costs 1.25 times the input price, or twice for the one-hour cache. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
